page_placements.theme: Neuron concept labels, selectivity and interpretability scores depend on the method

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that neuron-explanation scores change with the explainer and testing procedure, and argues that one-shot scores can underestimate how much activation variation is explainable. This refines the measurement-dependent version of the claim, but it does not directly test whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: The study measures how well generated explanations predict GPT-2 XL neuron activations. Its reported score comparisons bear narrowly on V7. It does not measure polysemanticity or test whether the same neurons respond to unrelated inputs. The 0.3% figure for GPT-4 is attributed to the 2023 paper, not a result of this study. Other referenced studies and comments are not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The post reruns the 2023 OpenAI explain-and-simulate pipeline on 50 sampled GPT-2 XL neurons (layers 8-40), with Opus 5.5 in place of GPT-4. It measures how well generated explanations predict activations. It never classifies neurons as polysemantic or monosemantic. It does not test whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, and it does not vary the activation range or the scoring rule used to call a neuron polysemantic. A low explanation score can come from a hard-to-describe single feature as easily as from a mixture. So the construct, explainability by an LLM explainer and simulator, is related to the claim but different from it. Changing the explainer model changes the explainer's skill, not how polysemanticity is defined or scored. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author concludes that Opus 5.5 explains sampled GPT-2 XL neurons far better than GPT-4: 3-19% identified depending on threshold, and 8% against the cited 0.3%. Under a one-sentence-per-neuron criterion GPT-2 XL is not clean. One-shot explanations are a lower bound, and asking LLMs to explain neurons is a promising direction.
record.recipe_differences: The post describes a rerun of the 2023 neuron-explanation procedure, but uses Opus 5.5 instead of GPT-4, 35 rather than 5 examples for explanation, permits multi-sentence explanations, uses subagents, batches neurons, and asks Opus for a 0-to-10 simulation score rather than GPT-4 probability-weighted expected values. It samples neurons rather than running the procedure on all GPT-2 XL neurons.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with explainer/simulator choice, pipeline development versus fresh neurons, and one-shot versus further targeted testing.

fits_no_version.finding: On the same 20 GPT-2 XL neurons, Opus 5.5 explanations scored higher than GPT-4 on every neuron. Across 50 sampled neurons, an estimated 3-19% (8% at one threshold) reach the explanation-score criteria. The fresh-neuron mean was 0.41 against 0.51 on the development set.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The measured share of 'well-explained' language-model neurons depends strongly on the explainer model used in automated interpretability pipelines.

fits_no_version.finding: For one hard neuron (L21 N4526), extended targeted investigation raised explained activation variation from 3.5% to 8%. The neuron nonetheless remained largely unexplained.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: One-shot automated neuron explanations underestimate how much of a neuron's activation can be explained.

record.problems: The study samples only 50 neurons from layers 8-40 rather than all GPT-2 XL neurons. The pipeline was designed on the first 20 neurons, and the fresh 30 had a lower mean score. Opus was given more examples and allowed longer explanations than GPT-4; simulation procedures also differed. The author notes possible language-model self-judging. The reported results do not directly measure polysemanticity, and several figure values are not stated numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numerical results were left out. Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 show per-neuron scores, but the text does not provide their individual values; the textual aggregate comparison and stated aggregates are recorded instead.

untested.parts: No count or share of GPT-2 XL neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and no layer comparison of polysemanticity.
No initialization, regularization or noise manipulation. A commenter raises dropout, but this is not tested.
No architecture, activation-function or regularization comparison.

The study does not examine whether apparently mixed activations share one feature. The L21 N4526 'meta, author talks to audience' grouping is anecdotal and not framed as reinterpreting a polysemantic neuron.

No variation of the examined activation range, and no comparison of scoring rules for labelling neurons polysemantic. Only the explainer model and the depth of investigation vary, under a fixed top-activation correlation metric.

missing.what: Share of the 50 neurons above each of the four score thresholds in Fig. 3. The TLDR range is 3-19%, but r2 records only 8% without its threshold.

record.verdict_notes: LessWrong post, not peer reviewed, small sample (50 neurons). The comparison to 0.3% uses a cited result from a different, full-scale run with fewer examples and single-sentence explanations. A top commenter (leogao) criticizes the top-activation correlation metric for ignoring recall. That critique is a comment, not a result of this study. No original source of the claim is involved.

versions.untested_parts: No vision model or mixed-input neuron response is tested.
Although GPT-2 XL is a language model, the study does not test whether MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, or estimate their share.
No feature-to-neuron capacity pressure or superposition mechanism is tested.
Initialization, regularization, and training noise are not tested as causes of polysemanticity.
No activation-function, architecture, or regularization comparison is made, and performance costs of reducing polysemanticity are not measured.
The study does not investigate whether apparently mixed inputs share one feature or job.

The study compares explanation-generation and testing procedures, but does not compare alternative definitions of polysemanticity, systematically vary the examined activation range, or measure how many neurons count as polysemantic under different scoring rules.

relation.reason: The post asks whether GPT-2 XL neurons are interpretable ('clean') but measures only explainer quality. It does not test polysemanticity, so 'tests' does not apply.

tranche.reason: The post reruns the explain-and-simulate pipeline with Opus 5.5 as explainer and simulator. It measures explanation quality but never classifies neurons as polysemantic or monosemantic, so it tests no version. The reader's earlier T5 call was wrong.

source_check.notes: The 8% vs 0.3% comparison mixes thresholds and coverage (OpenAI: all layers at >=0.8; here n=50 from layers 8-40, threshold unstated). The 20-neuron Opus vs GPT-4 gap also changes the simulator, 35 vs 5 examples and multi-sentence explanations. The fresh 30 neurons (mean 0.41 vs 0.51) were run in batches, which the author says lowered simulator scores slightly.

statements.problem: None. The text does not say which threshold gives 8%, and the statement's 'at one threshold' does not claim one. The 20-neuron comparison is of whole pipelines (explainer plus simulator), and the text calls the metric 'explanation score'.
